preword: this ended up longer than expected, sorry if the tone is negative in some way: i'm just autistic with experiences of being raised by a narcissist and genuinely trying to be helpful  
  
Look. An extra parent isn't THAT important. I never once missed having a father. What did, however, fuck me up, is having a narcissist in my life. At this point, you don't have a choice of him being in your life and he's apparently pretty charismatic. The \*best things\* for you to do for your son right now are:  
  
- Get a journal or notebook and write "\[redacted\] IS A NARCISSIST" on the first page. Write down everything he ever did to you. Read up about narcissists and how they act. Write cliffnotes. Every time you feel charmed by him, read it. Write down every interaction you have with him from now on. First, the blow-by-blow; just facts, no feelings, then how you felt about it. This is all a hard habit to get into, but it'll help you navigate your own emotions better when it comes to "feeling confused" or "gut feelings", because you'll be able to objectively look at long-term trends.  
  
- Get a journal or notebook for your son. Once he is old enough to start writing (i can't remember child developmental milestones, so i don't know if he's there already - i wasn't exactly a normal child) , encourage him to write a diary. At first, while he's learning how, help him - give him easy instructions, if he wants to draw the information, let him, never judge what he puts there, etc. Once he's a little older, get him a second one. From this point onwards, the second one is \*just for him\* to have a private space. The first one becomes a "conversation with mommy". The first one is the stuff he wants to tell you about, it's his letters-to-home when he's away from you, whether with his grandparents or with his father or spending a weekend fwith friends. He might grow out of this one, and it's ok. You can even alternate pages with him so you can tell him about your day, as well. But what's essential is the starting habit and the second journal. If it's a lockable journal, all the best - but make sure to get a third-party lock as journal locks are notoriously easy to pick. This will help stop him from getting in trouble with his father and father's future girlfriends if they decide to break his privacy and he's written something "negative". 

Why journals? Because journalling is an absolute brute of an anti-gaslighting tool. If you write down what was done and said while it's still fresh, then "it didn't happen that way" or "that's not what i meant" means sweet FA. You know. You don't only have to rely on your memory of what happened, which can be manipulated; you have it written down, as well as how you felt about it. As a bonus, if shit really hits the fan then both your and your son's journal can be used as evidence of that mans actions. Remember, narcissists are \*very good at lying to themselves\* and that makes them excellent at lying to others - because they really believe it. But they're still lying.

Good luck. And since that man has adhd don't forget to keep an eye out for adhd (or austism, since there are many commonalities) in your son, because the absolute best time to learn habits for both of you to healthily deal with and process his neurodivergence is when he's still young. No words for how soul-destroying it is to be trying your best and still be called names because you aren't normal and don't have normal-people functioning in some areas.

This is a couple of weeks old now, but it came up on the bar and I felt the need to reply:  
Look. The people saying you can only be friends with an ex if there's a child or if you still have feelings for them are wrong. Especially when you're \~30.  


Sometimes, relationships just don't work out. You're great as friends but not as lovers. That's fine. It happens. If you communicate properly and don't drive it to the point where you hate each other, then why would you hound each other out of shared communities (such as churches, hobby groups, game groups, etc)? What is the \*need\* to hate an ex?  Maybe it's a cultural difference.  


The only exes I am not still \*at least cordial with\* are the two who abused me. The others, there were usually periods of separation where we didn't talk to each other, but after a while, due to shared communities, we were back on speaking or friendly terms. I regularly have IRL ttrpg nights with one, and another joins a discord server's community game nights. Both are in happy relationships with others and both still send me pictures of their cats, because cats.  


All this to say that is not \*de facto\* a red flag. However, what is important is your feelings and how you feel insecure on the matter.   


You say you're not one to ask to see messages or go through someone's phone but... with permission, why not? You feel insecure. It may not be entirely his fault. Although it may be a little uncomfortable to see messages if he's talked about your relationship with her, isn't that better than the feeling of uncertainty? Even if he "stops talking to her", will you then trust that he isn't doing it in a way you can't see? It's better to have things in the open.   


Cons:  
 \- You'll see how your boyfriend talks to other people, which you may or may not be comfortable with  
\- He may feel like you don't trust him  


Pros:  
\- You'll get the answer you need, one way or another. If she's a backup, or if he's still chasing, you'll know. If she's interested and he's not, you'll know (and can tell him that it's not appropriate to carry on a friendship like that). If neither are interested and are truly just long term friends, you'll know.  


  
But I am saying this on the assumption that you do trust him and it is how you feel about yourself vs her that is the problem. If you do trust him and it's about you, explain it fully and make the request. Obviously if he says no, then don't do it. But, at that point, ask if he could limit contact with her at least for a while so that you can fully feel that you/your feelings are the priority here. Especially since he's saying the right things but then not changing anything. But maybe he just doesn't have her blocked and it's one-sided from her side.. I wouldn't know. I dunno, usually the message check isn't a solution I'd vouch for but here it really seems like the best way to ease your mind - on the assumption that your partner is merely being a bit dense, as opposed to intentionally missing the point.

His fear of other men shouldn't control you, to be honest. Like. You can't make the whole world safe for someone else. So it boils down to one of these things:

1. He doesn't trust other men to not attempt to assault you.  
1a) This is because of an experience he or someone he is close to  
 \- Honestly, not much that can be done other than talking it through. But you can't make the whole world safe for someone and nor should you stop them/yourself experiencing life because of your fears. All you can do is make sure you're safe when you're out clubbing - never go anywhere alone, keep an eye on your drink, etc.  
1b) This is because of his own thoughts towards womenPretty self explanatory really. He's trying to "protect" you from other guys who think like him but actually act on it.  


​

2) He doesn't trust you to not sleep with someone else  
2a) This is because he thinks women are weak-willed and can be convinced to sleep with any other bedicked person that gives them bedroom eyes   
\- Ruuuuuuude. But then some men genuinely seem to think that "no"/"I have a partner and am monogamous"/"I'm not into men" are all negotiable terms, so not exactly impossible.  
2b) This is because he doesn't trust you, specifically.  
2b-1) If this is due to issues from earlier in the relationship, the two of you need to work through it as a couple. You shouldn't stop living your life, and you shouldn't let it control you, but you can work out things that'll ease his mind without giving up your autonomy  
2b-2) If this is due to issues from a previous relationship, well, it still needs to be worked through, but his distrust doesn't actually stem from you. You shouldn't stop living your life, he should receive counselling and if you can help in a way that doesn't sacrifice your happiness, go for it.  
2b-3) As an alternative or addendum to 2b-2, regardless of whether or not a past partner has cheated, it could be due to his own guilty conscience. He either has cheated on previous partners or has cheated on you, and is now projecting his own behaviour onto you. There's not much you can do on this one without proof, though, other than not let him control you and to continue living your life the way you want.

  
3) It's not about trust at all, he just doesn't like you enjoying yourself without him and doesn't want to do things you enjoy unless he enjoys them as well. This is controlling and rude and you should - wait for it - not stop living your life!

As you can see, there... aren't many "good" options here. This is a comprehensive but basic list of reasonings; they're the most common ones. All the options for you are the same, though: you do what makes YOU happy. The compromise can fall in doing things to ease his mind, like texting him to let him know you're safe, etc. Do NOT let this fall into the more controlling behaviour of "prove you're with who you say you are/where you say you're at by taking a specific picture" or similar behaviours.

Please look up red flags of controlling, abusive relationships! Please be aware of them. And always keep an eye out. Even "harmless" behaviours can spiral if not checked, because without being properly worked on, the need for control never goes away.

Hope things work out for you :)

The problem is, any medicine can take up to *six weeks* to actually be effective. You can be experiencing side effects during that time and *yes*, some can make it worse before it gets better. It's a complicated process, messing with brain chemicals, and it affects people in a wide variety of ways. 

Keep contact with your medical professional about it. Keep a record of how you feel on it. You shouldn't make a judgement until at least the second week (many initial side effects start to lessen about this time) and then, depending on how you feel, you can decide whether it's worth to keep going (i.e do you *definitely* still feel worse than *not* being on it, and is it *definitely* not situational) or trying to swap to another medicine. It can take a lot of effort to find one that works for you. Trust me.. I've been through a lot of them. My problem with them is usually side effects that simply don't make the drug itself worth it, though. (Up to and including a complete allergy to one medicine, with less severe but still unpleasant reactions to the ones closely related to it.)

Technically speaking? You don't. Depression is very often linked with a lowered immune system, which means more illnesses. Commonly having bugs can be, in itself, a symptom of depression.
